source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 8 (PDF 180-204, printed 177-201); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 8 (Plant Physiology), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 A substance that provides the body with essential ingredients required for metabolism is called a:
blocks.explanation: A nutrient provides the body with essential ingredients required for metabolism (8.1).

book_ref.quote: A nutrient is a substance that provides the body with essential ingredients required for metabolism

blocks.prompt: 2 Which group of nutrients serves as sources of energy?
blocks.explanation: Carbohydrates, lipids and proteins are sources of energy; water, electrolytes, minerals and vitamins are needed for the metabolic process (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Specific nutrients, such as carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins, serve as sources of energy

blocks.prompt: 3 The collective processes involved in the intake and utilization of nutrients for growth, repair and maintenance are called:
blocks.explanation: Nutrition is the collective processes of intake and utilization of nutrients for growth, repair and maintenance (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Nutrition refers to the collective processes involved in the intake and utilization of nutrients

blocks.prompt: 4 How many macronutrients are there for plants?
blocks.explanation: There are nine macronutrients: C, H, O, N, K, Ca, P, Mg and S (8.1).

book_ref.quote: There are nine macronutrients

blocks.prompt: 5 How many micronutrients are named for plants?
blocks.explanation: There are seven micronutrients: iron, manganese, zinc, molybdenum, copper, chlorine and boron (8.1).

book_ref.quote: There are seven micronutrients

blocks.prompt: 6 Which one of the following is a micronutrient?
blocks.explanation: Boron is one of the seven micronutrients; potassium, calcium and sulphur are macronutrients (8.1).

book_ref.quote: iron, manganese, zinc, molybdenum, copper, chlorine, and boron

blocks.prompt: 7 Which element constitutes the core of the chlorophyll molecule?
blocks.explanation: Magnesium constitutes the core of the chlorophyll molecule and is therefore essential for photosynthesis (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Magnesium constitutes the core of the chlorophyll molecule

blocks.prompt: 8 Which macronutrient is a part of ATP and promotes root growth?
blocks.explanation: Phosphorus is a part of ATP; it promotes root growth and favours flowering (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Phosphorus is a part of ATP

blocks.prompt: 9 A deficiency of nitrogen in plants results in:

options.text: premature falling of leaves and delayed maturity

blocks.explanation: Nitrogen deficiency results in leaf loss and stunted growth (8.1).

book_ref.quote: A deficiency of nitrogen results in leaf loss and stunted growth

blocks.prompt: 10 Dark patches are formed on the leaves when there is a shortage of:
blocks.explanation: Shortage of potassium forms dark patches on the leaves (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Dark patches are formed on the leaves when there is shortage of potassium

blocks.prompt: 11 Which element provides stability to the cell wall and aids in the development of seeds?
blocks.explanation: Calcium stabilizes and develops the cell wall and aids seed development; its shortage causes yellow and brown patches (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Calcium provides stability to the cell wall and promotes the development of the cell wall

blocks.prompt: 12 Which element is fundamental in the metabolism of nitrogen, and its shortage makes the plant lighter in colour?
blocks.explanation: Sulfur is a fundamental element in nitrogen metabolism; its shortage makes the plant lighter in colour (8.1).

book_ref.quote: If there is a shortage of sulfur, the plant becomes lighter in colour

blocks.prompt: 13 Interveinal chlorosis results from the deficiency of:
blocks.explanation: Iron is essential for chlorophyll synthesis; its deficiency results in interveinal chlorosis (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Its deficiency results in interveinal chlorosis

blocks.prompt: 14 Premature falling of the leaf and delayed maturity are caused by the deficiency of:
blocks.explanation: Manganese deficiency results in premature leaf fall and delayed maturity (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Its deficiency results in the premature falling of the leaf and delayed maturity

blocks.prompt: 15 Manganese is important for the activity of which antioxidant enzyme?
blocks.explanation: Manganese is important for antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, which help mitigate oxidative stress (8.1).

book_ref.quote: such as superoxide dismutase (SOD)

blocks.prompt: 16 Which micronutrient facilitates chlorophyll synthesis, root development and uptake of nutrients?
blocks.explanation: Zinc facilitates chlorophyll synthesis, root development and nutrient uptake; its deficiency can cause stunted growth (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Zinc facilitates chlorophyll synthesis, root development and uptake of nutrients

blocks.prompt: 17 Which micronutrient is critical for nitrogen fixation and nitrogen reduction?
blocks.explanation: Molybdenum is critical for nitrogen fixation, nitrogen reduction, sulfur and phosphorus metabolism and iron utilization (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Molybdenum is critical for nitrogen fixation

blocks.prompt: 18 Which element is necessary for lignin synthesis, giving strength and rigidity to the cell wall?
blocks.explanation: Copper is necessary for lignin synthesis, which provides strength and rigidity to the cell wall (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Copper is necessary for lignin synthesis

blocks.prompt: 19 Which micronutrient is involved in stomatal regulation and osmotic adjustment?
blocks.explanation: Chlorine is involved in stomatal regulation, osmotic adjustment and transport of nutrients (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Chlorine is involved in stomatal regulation, osmotic adjustment and transport of nutrients

blocks.prompt: 20 Insectivorous plants are:
blocks.explanation: All insectivorous plants are true autotrophs; their development only accelerates when they capture prey (8.1).

book_ref.quote: All insectivorous plants are true autotrophs

blocks.prompt: 21 Insectivorous plants mainly benefit from which compounds of the animal body?
blocks.explanation: Apparently the nitrogenous compounds of the animal body benefit insectivorous plants (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Apparently, nitrogenous compounds of animal body are of benefit to these plants

blocks.prompt: 22 In the pitcher plant, the pitcher is a modified:
blocks.explanation: Pitcher plant has leaves modified into a sac or pitcher partly filled with water; the leaf's terminal portion forms a hood (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Pitcher plant has leaves modified into a sac or a pitcher

blocks.prompt: 23 In the pitcher plant, insects are prevented from crawling out of the pitcher by:
blocks.explanation: The pitcher has numerous stiff hairs that prevent little insects from crawling out once they fall inside (8.1).

book_ref.quote: It has numerous stiff hairs that prevent little insects from crawling out

blocks.prompt: 24 In Venus-fly trap, the lobes close rapidly when prey touches:

options.text: the stiff hairs of the pitcher
trichomes on the inner surfaces of the lobes
the drop of dew at the leaf tip

blocks.explanation: Trichomes (hair-like projections) on the inner surfaces of the lobes trigger the lobes to close rapidly on contact with prey (8.1).

book_ref.quote: which are hair-like projections that trigger the lobes to close rapidly upon contact with prey

blocks.prompt: 25 In Venus-fly trap, the prey is prevented from escaping because:

options.text: fine bristles lining the trap interlock on closure
stiff hairs point downwards in a pitcher

blocks.explanation: The hinged traps are lined with fine bristles that interlock upon closure, preventing the prey from escaping (8.1).

book_ref.quote: The hinged traps are lined with fine bristles that interlock upon closure

blocks.prompt: 26 Which insectivorous plant catches its prey with shiny drops of "dew" on tentacle-like hairs?
blocks.explanation: Sundew catches prey with shiny drops of dew; insects attracted by its odour are trapped by tentacles (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Sundew catches its prey with shiny drops of

blocks.prompt: 27 Stomata are typically found in:

options.text: leaves, and even in some stems

blocks.explanation: Stomata are typically found in leaves but can even be present in some stems (8.2).

book_ref.quote: These are typically found in leaves but can even be present in some stems

blocks.prompt: 28 Guard cells of stomata are:
blocks.explanation: Guard cells are bean-shaped and contain chloroplasts (8.2).

book_ref.quote: Guard cells are bean-shaped and contain chloroplasts

blocks.prompt: 29 The opening and closing of stomata control the rate of:
blocks.explanation: The opening and closing of stomata control the transpiration rate in plants (8.2).

book_ref.quote: The opening and closing of stomata control the transpiration rate in plants

blocks.prompt: 30 Stomata typically close at night in order to:
blocks.explanation: At night photosynthesis ceases, so stomata typically close to conserve water; respiration still continues (8.2).

book_ref.quote: At night, when photosynthesis ceases due to lack of light, stomata typically close to conserve water

blocks.prompt: 31 Guard cells function as:
blocks.explanation: The guard cells function as multisensory hydraulic valves (8.2).

book_ref.quote: The guard cells function as multisensory hydraulic valves

blocks.prompt: 32 The starch sugar hypothesis of stomatal movement was proposed in 1856 by:
blocks.explanation: In 1856 the German botanist H. Van Mohl proposed the starch sugar hypothesis (8.2).

book_ref.quote: In 1856, German botanist H. Van Mohl proposed

blocks.prompt: 33 According to the starch sugar hypothesis, stomata close at night because:

options.text: K⁺ is actively pumped into the guard cells
sugars become insoluble starch or are respired, so water leaves the guard cells
blue light acidifies the guard cells
abscisic acid pumps K⁺ into the guard cells

blocks.explanation: At night sugars are converted to insoluble starch or used in respiration; free sugars decline, water moves out and the guard cells become flaccid (8.2).

book_ref.quote: At night, photosynthesis ceases, and sugars are converted to insoluble starch or used for respiration

blocks.prompt: 34 The weakness of the starch sugar hypothesis is that it does not fully explain:

options.text: the presence of chloroplasts in guard cells
the closing of stomata at night
the entry of CO₂ through stomata
the rapid turgor changes in guard cells

blocks.explanation: The starch sugar mechanism does not fully explain the rapid turgor changes in guard cells during stomatal movements (8.2).

book_ref.quote: However, this mechanism does not fully explain the rapid turgor changes in guard cells during stomatal movements

blocks.prompt: 35 According to the second hypothesis, stomata open because of the active transport of which ion into guard cells?
blocks.explanation: Active transport of K⁺ into guard cells reduces their osmotic potential; water enters by osmosis and the stomata open (8.2).

book_ref.quote: which reduces their osmotic potential

blocks.prompt: 36 Which light enhances K⁺ uptake by guard cells?
blocks.explanation: Blue light enhances the process by acidifying the surrounding environment, promoting K⁺ uptake and water absorption (8.2).

book_ref.quote: Blue light enhances this process by acidifying the surrounding environment

blocks.prompt: 37 At night, K⁺ leaves the guard cells by:
blocks.explanation: At night K⁺ passively diffuses out; water is lost, guard cells become flaccid and the stomata close (8.2).

book_ref.quote: At night, K⁺ passively diffuses out of the guard cells

blocks.prompt: 38 At high temperature, when leaf cells start wilting, the hormone released by mesophyll cells to close stomata is:
blocks.explanation: Abscisic acid stops the active transport of K⁺ into guard cells, overriding light and CO₂, so stomata close (8.2).

book_ref.quote: a hormone called abscisic acid, is released by mesophyll cells

blocks.prompt: 39 Palisade tissue of the leaf is located:
blocks.explanation: Palisade tissue lies just beneath the upper epidermis; its elongated, tightly packed cells are rich in chloroplasts (8.2).

book_ref.quote: Palisade tissue is primarily located just beneath the upper epidermis of the leaf

blocks.prompt: 40 After entering the leaf through stomata, CO₂ first travels through the air spaces of the:
blocks.explanation: CO₂ diffuses in through stomata, travels through air spaces of the spongy mesophyll and then into palisade cells for photosynthesis (8.2).

book_ref.quote: Once inside, the gas travels through air spaces within the spongy mesophyll

blocks.prompt: 41 The internal hydrostatic pressure that maintains the rigidity of parenchyma cells is called:
blocks.explanation: Water absorbed by parenchyma cells creates an internal hydrostatic pressure, the turgor pressure, which keeps the cells rigid (8.3).

book_ref.quote: This water creates an internal hydrostatic pressure known as turgor pressure

blocks.prompt: 42 The membrane that surrounds the vacuole is called:
blocks.explanation: The tonoplast surrounds the vacuole; its active transport moves ions into the vacuole (8.3).

book_ref.quote: The membrane that surrounds the vacuole is called the tonoplast

blocks.prompt: 43 Which supporting cells lack secondary walls and have primary walls thickened at the corners?
blocks.explanation: Collenchyma cells lack secondary walls; their primary walls are thickened at the corners (8.3).

book_ref.quote: Collenchyma cells lack secondary walls

blocks.prompt: 44 The corners of collenchyma walls are thickened due to extra deposition of:
blocks.explanation: Collenchyma primary walls are thickened at the corners due to extra deposition of cellulose (8.3).

book_ref.quote: Their primary walls are thickened at the corners, due to extra deposition of cellulose

blocks.prompt: 45 Collenchyma is found:

options.text: in seed coats and shells of nuts
in the pith of old woody stems
beneath the epidermis of young stems and leaf stalks
in the cork of the bark

blocks.explanation: Collenchyma lies beneath the epidermis of young stems, leaf stalks and along leaf veins (8.3).

book_ref.quote: They are found beneath the epidermis of young stems, leaf stalks and along veins in leaves

blocks.prompt: 46 The thick secondary walls of sclerenchyma are saturated with:
blocks.explanation: Sclerenchyma walls are saturated with lignin, an organic compound that confers strength and rigidity (8.3).

book_ref.quote: These walls are saturated with lignin

blocks.prompt: 47 The majority of sclerenchyma cells are:
blocks.explanation: The majority of sclerenchyma cells are non-living; the tissue's main function is support (8.3).

book_ref.quote: The majority of sclerenchyma cells are non-living

blocks.prompt: 48 Sclereids are present in:

options.text: beneath the epidermis of young stems
seed coats and shells of nuts

blocks.explanation: Sclereids are smaller than fibres and are present in seed coats and shells of nuts; their function is protection (8.3).

book_ref.quote: are present in the seed coats and shells of nuts

blocks.prompt: 49 Water potential is symbolized by the Greek letter:
blocks.explanation: Water potential is symbolized by the Greek letter psi, Ψw (8.4).

book_ref.quote: symbolized by Greek letter psi

blocks.prompt: 50 The water potential of pure water is, by definition:
blocks.explanation: Pure water has the maximum water potential, which by definition is zero (8.4).

book_ref.quote: Pure water has maximum water potential which by definition is zero

blocks.prompt: 51 At atmospheric pressure, the water potential of any solution is:

options.text: higher than that of pure water

blocks.explanation: All solutions have lower Ψw than pure water and so have negative Ψw (8.4).

book_ref.quote: All solutions have lower Ψw than pure water

blocks.prompt: 52 In terms of water potential, osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from:
blocks.explanation: Osmosis is the movement of water from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane (8.4).

book_ref.quote: So, the osmosis can be defined as the movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential

blocks.prompt: 53 If more solute molecules are present, the solute potential becomes:
blocks.explanation: Ψs is always negative; more solute molecules make Ψs lower (more negative) (8.4).

book_ref.quote: Ψs is always a negative value

blocks.prompt: 54 If pressure greater than atmospheric pressure is applied to a solution, its water potential:
blocks.explanation: Pressure greater than atmospheric pressure increases water potential; this part is the pressure potential (8.4).

book_ref.quote: If pressure greater than atmospheric pressure is applied to pure water or a solution, its water potential increases

blocks.prompt: 55 The total water potential of a plant cell is given by:
blocks.explanation: Total water potential is the sum of solute potential and pressure potential: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp (8.4).

book_ref.quote: Thus, the total water potential (Ψw) is sum of solute potential

blocks.prompt: 56 The flow of water along a water potential gradient is faster when the gradient is:
blocks.explanation: The steeper the potential gradient, the faster the flow of water along it (8.4).

book_ref.quote: The steeper the potential gradient the faster is the flow of water along it

blocks.prompt: 57 Root hairs are extensions of the root's:
blocks.explanation: Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells of roots; most uptake of water and minerals takes place through them (8.5).

book_ref.quote: which are actually extensions of epidermal cells of roots

blocks.prompt: 58 The apoplast pathway becomes discontinuous in the endodermis due to:
blocks.explanation: The apoplast pathway becomes discontinuous in the endodermis due to the Casparian segments (8.5).

book_ref.quote: The apoplast pathway becomes discontinuous in the endodermis

blocks.prompt: 59 The pathway of water through the system of adjacent cell walls of root cells is the:
blocks.explanation: The apoplast pathway is a continuous pathway of adjacent cell walls in roots (8.5).

book_ref.quote: It is a continuous pathway that involves a system of adjacent cell walls in the plant roots

blocks.prompt: 60 Plasmodesmata are:

options.text: bands of suberin in the endodermis
cytoplasmic strands through pores in adjacent cell walls

blocks.explanation: Plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic strands through pores in adjacent cell walls; they link protoplasts in the symplast pathway (8.5).

book_ref.quote: which are cytoplasmic strands that extend through pores in adjacent cell walls

blocks.prompt: 61 Movement of water through which pathway in roots is negligible?
blocks.explanation: In the vacuolar pathway water moves from vacuole to vacuole; this movement is negligible (8.5).

book_ref.quote: Movement in vacuolar pathway is negligible

blocks.prompt: 62 Which one of the following is NOT a component of xylem?
blocks.explanation: Xylem comprises tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma; companion cells belong to phloem (8.5).

book_ref.quote: Xylem comprises of tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma

blocks.prompt: 63 Tracheids are linked to each other by:
blocks.explanation: Tracheids have tapered ends and are linked by bordered pits, which allow lateral movement of water (8.5).

book_ref.quote: they are linked to each other by bordered pits

blocks.prompt: 64 Compared to tracheids, vessels are:
blocks.explanation: Vessels are shorter and broader than tracheids and form continuous channels (8.5).

book_ref.quote: Vessels are shorter and broader compared to tracheids

blocks.prompt: 65 The living, thin-walled component of xylem that takes part in lateral translocation is:
blocks.explanation: Xylem parenchyma are living thin-walled cells that store nutrients and water and take part in lateral translocation (8.5).

book_ref.quote: Xylem parenchyma are living cells with thin walls

blocks.prompt: 66 In the TACT mechanism, the letter 'A' stands for:
blocks.explanation: TACT stands for Transpiration, Adhesion, Cohesion and Tension (8.5).

book_ref.quote: The TACT (Transpiration, Adhesion, Cohesion, Tension) mechanism

blocks.prompt: 67 The primary driving force behind water transport in the xylem is:
blocks.explanation: Transpiration creates negative pressure in the leaf that pulls water up; it is the primary driving force (8.5).

book_ref.quote: Transpiration, therefore, act as the primary driving force behind water transport in the xylem

blocks.prompt: 68 The attraction between water molecules and the walls of xylem vessels is called:
blocks.explanation: Adhesion is the attraction between water molecules and xylem walls; it prevents breaks in the water column (8.5).

book_ref.quote: Adhesion is the attraction between water molecules and the walls of the xylem vessels

blocks.prompt: 69 Cohesion between water molecules is caused by:
blocks.explanation: Cohesion is the attraction between water molecules themselves, caused by hydrogen bonding (8.5).

book_ref.quote: Cohesion refers to the attractive force between water molecules themselves, caused by hydrogen bonding

blocks.prompt: 70 In the TACT mechanism, tension is:

options.text: the pressure of water entering roots
the attraction of water to xylem walls
the negative pressure created by the pull of transpiration

blocks.explanation: Tension is the negative pressure created by the pulling force of transpiration; it pulls the cohesive water column upwards (8.5).

book_ref.quote: Tension is the negative pressure created by the pulling force of the transpiration at the leaf level

blocks.prompt: 71 In plants with secondary growth, phloem constitutes the:
blocks.explanation: Phloem lies on the outer side of the vascular tissue and constitutes the inner bark (8.6).

book_ref.quote: The phloem constitutes the inner bark

blocks.prompt: 72 'Sieve areas' of sieve tube elements are:

options.text: portions of the cell wall where pores interconnect the elements

blocks.explanation: Sieve areas are portions of the cell wall where pores interconnect the sieve tube elements (8.6).

book_ref.quote: Sieve tube elements have 'sieve areas'

blocks.prompt: 73 Companion cells supply which of the following to sieve tube elements?
blocks.explanation: Companion cells, linked by plasmodesmata, supply ATP and proteins to sieve tube elements (8.6).

book_ref.quote: Companion cells supply ATP and proteins to sieve tube elements

blocks.prompt: 74 Sugars, resins, latex and mucilage are stored in phloem by:
blocks.explanation: Phloem parenchyma stores sugars, resins, latex and mucilage, important for defence and moisture retention (8.6).

book_ref.quote: Phloem parenchyma stores substances, such as sugars, resins, latex, and mucilage

blocks.prompt: 75 On average, sugar moves in the phloem at a velocity of about:
blocks.explanation: Sugar moves in phloem at about 1 meter per hour, while diffusion is 1 meter per eight years; so diffusion is far too slow (8.6).

book_ref.quote: which on the average is 1 meter per hour

blocks.prompt: 76 The pressure-flow theory was proposed by:
blocks.explanation: The pressure-flow (mass-flow) theory was proposed by Ernst Munch in 1930 (8.6).

book_ref.quote: This theory was proposed by Ernst Munch in 1930

blocks.prompt: 77 In translocation, a 'sink' is the region where sugars are:
blocks.explanation: Translocation moves sugar from the source (where synthesized) to the sink (where consumed or stored) (8.6).

book_ref.quote: This process of translocation moves sugar from the source

blocks.prompt: 78 Excess glucose of mesophyll cells is converted into which sugar for translocation?
blocks.explanation: Excess glucose is converted into the non-reducing sugar sucrose, which is translocated (8.6).

book_ref.quote: The excess of glucose is converted into non-reducing sugar i.e., sucrose

blocks.prompt: 79 Sucrose moves from mesophyll cells into the companion cells of phloem by:
blocks.explanation: Sucrose is actively transported into companion cells and then diffuses to sieve tubes through plasmodesmata (8.6).

book_ref.quote: Sucrose is actively transported from mesophyll cells to the companion cells of phloem

blocks.prompt: 80 From companion cells, sucrose reaches the sieve tubes through:
blocks.explanation: Sucrose diffuses from companion cells into sieve tubes through plasmodesmata, raising its concentration there (8.6).

book_ref.quote: From here, sucrose diffuses to sieve tubes, through plasmodesmata

blocks.prompt: 81 Growth in plants refers to:

options.text: a temporary increase in water content

blocks.explanation: Growth in plants is a permanent increase in size, in height, width and mass (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Growth in plants refers to a permanent increase in size

blocks.prompt: 82 In higher plants, growth is limited to certain regions called:
blocks.explanation: In higher plants growth is limited to growing points, made of meristems capable of continuous cell division (8.7).

book_ref.quote: growth is limited to certain regions known as growing points

blocks.prompt: 83 Meristems situated at the bases of internodes, as in grasses, are:
blocks.explanation: Intercalary meristems are separated from the apex by permanent tissues and lie at the bases of internodes, e.g., grasses (8.7).

book_ref.quote: They are situated at the bases of internodes in many plants such as grasses

blocks.prompt: 84 Which type of meristem is temporary?
blocks.explanation: Intercalary meristems are temporary, whereas apical meristems are perpetual growth zones (8.7).

book_ref.quote: play an important role in the production of leaves and flower. These are temporary

blocks.prompt: 85 Perpetual growth zones that increase the number of cells at the tips of roots and stems are:
blocks.explanation: Apical meristems at root and shoot tips are perpetual growth zones and play an important role in primary growth (8.7).

book_ref.quote: These are perpetual growth zones found and are responsible for the increase in the number of cells

blocks.prompt: 86 Vascular cambium is located:

options.text: in the outer layer of stems

blocks.explanation: Vascular cambium lies between xylem and phloem and produces secondary xylem and secondary phloem (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Vascular cambium is located between the xylem and phloem

blocks.prompt: 87 Which tissue produces cork cells that replace the epidermis and form the outer protective bark?
blocks.explanation: Cork cambium forms in the outer layer of stems and roots and produces cork cells that replace the epidermis (8.7).

book_ref.quote: This tissue produces cork cells which replace the epidermis

blocks.prompt: 88 Primary growth is responsible for an increase in:
blocks.explanation: Primary growth increases the length of plants and is due to apical meristems (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Primary growth is responsible for an increase in the length of the plants

blocks.prompt: 89 Small, non-vacuolated cells with spherical nuclei in the centre of the cytoplasm are found in the zone of:
blocks.explanation: In the zone of cell division cells are non-vacuolated and small, with spherical nuclei in the centre (8.7).

book_ref.quote: In this zone, cells are non-vacuolated and small

blocks.prompt: 90 Large vacuolated cells with nuclei in the peripheries of the cytoplasm occur in the zone of:
blocks.explanation: In the zone of cell elongation cells are vacuolated and large, with nuclei at the peripheries (8.7).

book_ref.quote: They have nuclei in the peripheries of cytoplasm

blocks.prompt: 91 During cell elongation, the cell wall:

options.text: becomes more plastic and wall pressure is reduced

blocks.explanation: During elongation the volume increases by water uptake; plasticity of the cell wall increases and wall pressure is reduced (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Plasticity of cell wall increases and wall pressure is reduced

blocks.prompt: 92 Secondary growth is due to the activity of:
blocks.explanation: Secondary growth increases thickness of stems and roots through the lateral meristems, vascular cambium and cork cambium (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Secondary growth refers to the increase in thickness or girth of stems and roots

blocks.prompt: 93 Cells produced on the inner margin of the vascular cambium make:
blocks.explanation: Outer margin cells make secondary phloem and inner margin cells make secondary xylem (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Cells produced on outer margins of vascular cambium make secondary phloem

blocks.prompt: 94 The region of a mature stem outside the vascular cambium, containing secondary phloem, cork cambium and cork, is called:
blocks.explanation: Secondary phloem, cork cambium and cork outside the vascular cambium together are called bark (8.7).

book_ref.quote: which contains secondary phloem, cork cambium and cork, is collectively called bark

blocks.prompt: 95 Spring wood is lighter in colour because in spring the cambium produces:

options.text: a large volume of xylem with wider vessels
fewer, narrower and denser xylem elements

blocks.explanation: In spring the active cambium produces a large volume of xylem with wider vessels, giving lighter spring wood (8.7).

book_ref.quote: resulting in lighter-coloured spring wood

blocks.prompt: 96 The scientific method of dating and studying tree rings to analyse past climate is called:
blocks.explanation: Dendrochronology dates and studies tree rings to analyse past climate conditions and events (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Dendrochronology is the scientific method of dating and studying tree rings

blocks.prompt: 97 In an annual ring, the change from autumn wood to the next year's spring wood is:
blocks.explanation: The transition from spring to autumn wood is gradual, but from autumn back to spring it is abrupt, marking the ring boundary (8.7).

book_ref.quote: but the shift from autumn back to spring in the following year is abrupt

blocks.prompt: 98 How many major groups of plant growth regulators are there?
blocks.explanation: Five major groups: auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, abscisic acid and ethylene (8.7).

book_ref.quote: There are five major groups of plant growth regulators

blocks.prompt: 99 Which growth regulator promotes apical dominance and inhibits abscission?
blocks.explanation: Auxins (IAA) promote apical dominance and fruit growth and inhibit abscission (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Promote apical dominance and fruit growth

blocks.prompt: 100 Auxins affect root growth in which way?

options.text: promote it only at high concentrations
promote it at very low and inhibit it at higher concentrations

blocks.explanation: In root, auxins promote growth at very low concentrations and inhibit it at higher concentrations, e.g., geotropism (8.7).

book_ref.quote: In root, promote growth at very low concentrations

blocks.prompt: 101 How many different gibberellins are known, according to the chapter?
blocks.explanation: Gibberellins contain gibberellic acid and there are more than 110 different gibberellins (8.7).

book_ref.quote: there are more than 110 different gibberellins

blocks.prompt: 102 'Bolting' of some rosette plants is promoted by:
blocks.explanation: Gibberellins promote bolting of some rosette plants (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Promote ‘bolting’ of some rosette plants

blocks.prompt: 103 Gibberellins may substitute for red light; therefore they:

options.text: promote flowering in short-day plants only
promote flowering in long-day plants and inhibit it in short-day plants
promote flowering only in day-neutral plants

blocks.explanation: Gibberellins may substitute for red light, so they promote flowering in long-day plants and inhibit it in short-day plants (8.7).

book_ref.quote: Sometimes may substitute for red light

blocks.prompt: 104 Which growth regulator promotes cytokinesis and increases the rate of DNA replication?
